			- Autochrome Lumière (1907): This was the first commercially successful color process. It used a glass plate coated with microscopic grains of dyed potato starch (red, green, and blue) acting as color filters. Light passed through the grains and onto a black-and-white emulsion beneath. When developed, the image retained the colors.					- Autochrome Lumière (1907): This was the first commercially successful color process. 			[Technical note: In steady-state, the temperature at the surface of a Steppenwolf planet (Ts), i.e., the top of the ice or frozen gas layer, will be set by a balance between thermal emission and geothermal heat flux, F = σTs4, where σ is the Stefan–Boltzmann constant. Astrophysical radiation backgrounds (Mathis et al. 1983; Dole et al. 2006) are negligible. Any gas present in the atmosphere at planetary ejection or outgassed subsequently by geological processes will tend to freeze into a low-thermal-conductivity blanket that could allow T0 to exceed Ts. A blanket formed by freezing Earth’s current atmosphere would only increase T0 by about 4 K…Isostatic adjustment (Fowler 1990), however, will tend to cause some continents or islands to rise above the layers of water and ice on an Earth-like Steppenwolf planet with an active mantle, allowing volcanoes to continuously emit gasses that can freeze onto the water ice surface. Here, we will consider carbon dioxide because it is likely to be outgassed in significant quantities from an Earth-like planet and it supports a stable layer with relatively high base temperature relative to other common gases. To find the temperature at the carbon-dioxide layer base, we note that the thermal conductivity of car- bon dioxide again scales as T−1 (here, in a more lim- ited regime), but with constant of proportionality A ≈ 100 W m−1 (Sumarokov et al. 2003). We find that the maximum temperature supported is robustly ≈ 220 K for Earth-like Steppenwolf planets and is determined by the weak temperature dependence of the melting curve (Giordano et al. 2006). Setting T0 = 220 K reduces the required steady-state water-ice thickness by an order of magnitude. At Earth mass, the temperature at the bottom of a layer of solid CO2 reaches the melting temperature of CO2 for a layer thickness of ≈ 2 km, or ≈ 3×106 kg m−2. Venus’ atmosphere has a partial pressure of CO2 of ≈90 bar (≈ 106 kg m−2), which is roughly the vapor pressure of carbonate rocks at Venus’ surface tempera- ture, implying that there may be more carbon locked in rock in equilibrium with the atmosphere (Pierrehumbert 2010). The store of carbon in carbonate rocks in Earth’s interior is uncertain, but the continental crust is esti- mated to contain the equivalent of ≈ 7 × 105 kg m−2 CO2 and the mantle may contain 2–4 times this amount (Zhang & Zindler 1993). Therefore it appears reason- able to assume that a Steppenwolf planet could have a sufficient complement of CO2 to significantly elevate T0.  Since the viscosity of ice depends strongly on tem- perature (Barr & Showman 2009), if ice convection were to occur on a Steppenwolf planet, it would occur only in the lower, warmer ice regions and would be capped by a “stagnant” conducting lid (Solomatov 1995). …detection of reflected sunlight in the op- tical wavebands and IR follow-up present the only viable observational choices in the near term.  For a single-visit limiting magnitude r ≈ 24.7 of LSST (Jones et al. 2009) (and comparable r = 24 in the nearer-term Pan-STARRS (Jewitt 2003)), and albedo of 0.5, the limiting distance out to which an object can be detected with reflected sunlight is ≈ 830(r/R⊕)1/2 AU. The baseline requirement to identify a Steppenwolf planet is a detection of thermal emission in the far-IR. Photometric microlensing has also been proposed as a method to detect rogue planets throughout the galaxy (Han et al. 2004). If each stellar system ejects one M⊕ planet, a survey like the Galactic Exoplanet Survey Tele- scope could anticipate ∼20 detections of rogue planets…If a Steppenwolf planet harbors life, it could have origi- nated in a more benign era before ejection from the host star. Alternatively, after ejection, life could originate around hydrothermal vents, which are a proposed loca- tion for the origin of life on Earth (Baross & Hoffman 1985). If life can originate and survive on a Steppenwolf planet, it must be truly ubiquitous in the universe.]					[Technical note: In steady-state, the temperature at the surface of a Steppenwolf planet (Ts), i.e., the top of the ice or frozen gas layer, will be set by a balance between thermal emission and geothermal heat flux, F = σTs4, where σ is the Stefan–Boltzmann constant. 			[Technical note: Magnetic explosions—Periodically, a probe coming passing too deeply into Jupiter’s magnetosphere, or encountering magnetic anomalies, may explode due to its magnetic shielding deforming too quickly. Similarly, high currency spikes caused by magnetic induction can cause electronics to explode. “Magnetic reconnection could be the Universe's favorite way to make things explode…Magnetic lines of force cross, cancel, reconnect and—Bang! Magnetic energy is unleashed, with charged-particles flying off near the speed of light.” Jupiter's magnetic field is 20 times stronger than the magnetic field on Earth. Unexpected increases in the magnetic field can come as a result of interactions between the fields of Jupiter, its satellites’ fields, and the Sun’s field, sometimes causing a “foamy” texture to the field.]					[Technical note: Magnetic explosions—Periodically, a probe coming passing too deeply into Jupiter’s magnetosphere, or encountering magnetic anomalies, may explode due to its magnetic shielding deforming too quickly. Similarly, high currency spikes caused by magnetic induction can cause electronics to explode. “Magnetic reconnection could be the Universe's favorite way to make things explode…Magnetic lines of force cross, cancel, reconnect and—Bang! Magnetic energy is unleashed, with charged-particles flying off near the speed of light.” Jupiter's magnetic field is 20 times stronger than the magnetic field on Earth. Unexpected increases in the magnetic field can come as a result of interactions between the fields of Jupiter, its satellites’ fields, and the Sun’s field, sometimes causing a “foamy” texture to the field.]											
			[Technical note: NASA has speculated on the feasibility of mining the atmospheres of the outer planets, particularly for helium-3, an isotope of helium that is rare on Earth and could have a very high value per unit mass as thermonuclear fuel.[77] Factories stationed in orbit could mine the gas and deliver it to visiting craft.[79] However, the Jovian system in general poses particular disadvantages for colonization because of the severe radiation conditions prevailing in Jupiter's magnetosphere and the planet's particularly deep gravitational well. Jupiter would deliver about 36 Sv (3600 rem) per day to unshielded colonists at Io and about 5.4 Sv (540 rems) per day to unshielded colonists at Europa,[80] which is a decisive aspect due to the fact that already an exposure to about 0.75 Sv over a period of a few days is enough to cause radiation poisoning, and about 5 Sv over a few days is fatal.[80][81] In 2003, NASA conducted a conceptual study called "Human Outer Planets Exploration" (HOPE) regarding the future human exploration of the outer solar system. The possibility was mooted of building a surface base on Callisto, because of the low radiation levels at the moon's distance from Jupiter and its geological stability. Callisto is the only one of Jupiter's Galilean satellites for which human exploration is feasible. The levels of ionizing radiation on Io, Europa and Ganymede are inimical to human life, and adequate protective measures have yet to be devised.[80] Equipment sometimes requires isolation from external magnetic fields. For static or slowly varying magnetic fields (below about 100 kHz) the Faraday shielding described above is ineffective. In these cases shields made of high magnetic permeability metal alloys can be used, such as sheets of Permalloy and Mu-Metal,[5] or with nanocrystalline grain structure ferromagnetic metal coatings.[6] These materials don't block the magnetic field, as with electric shielding, but rather draw the field into themselves, providing a path for the magnetic field lines around the shielded volume. The best shape for magnetic shields is thus a closed container surrounding the shielded volume. The effectiveness of this type of shielding depends on the material's permeability, which generally drops off at both very low magnetic field strengths and at high field strengths where the material becomes saturated. So to achieve low residual fields, magnetic shields often consist of several enclosures one inside the other, each of which successively reduces the field inside it. Because of the above limitations of passive shielding, an alternative used with static or low-frequency fields is active shielding; using a field created by electromagnets to cancel the ambient field within a volume.[7] Solenoids and Helmholtz coils are types of coils that can be used for this purpose. Additionally, superconducting materials can expel magnetic fields via the Meissner effect. The squareness (saturation remanence divided by saturation magnetization) and coercivity are figures of merit for hard magnets although energy product (saturation magnetization times coercivity) is most commonly quoted. Magnetostriction (cf. electrostriction) is a property of ferromagnetic materials that causes them to change their shape or dimensions during the process of magnetization. The variation of materials' magnetization due to the applied magnetic field changes the magnetostrictive strain until reaching its saturation value, λ. This effect causes energy loss due to frictional heating in susceptible ferromagnetic cores. The effect is also responsible for the low-pitched humming sound that can be heard coming from transformers. Sendust is a magnetic metal powder that was invented by Hakaru Masumoto at Tohoku Imperial University in Sendai, Japan, about 1936 as an alternative to permalloy in inductor applications for telephone networks. Sendust cores have high magnetic permeability (up to 140 000), low loss, low coercivity (5 A/m) good temperature stability and saturation flux density up to 1 T. —Can a sintered sendust core explode due to overly high magnetic fields?— Hiding from Jupiter’s radiation: http://www.astrobio.net/news-exclusive/hiding-from-jupiters-radiation/ Jupiter is the largest planet in the solar system with a radius of over 70 000 km. While 20,000 times the intrinsic strength of Earth's magnetic dynamo is incredible, it is approximately a dipole field. Given that Jupiter's radius is almost 12 times that of Earth, and that dipole field strength drops off with the cube of the radius perpendicular to the dipole axis, one would project a surface field on the order of 7 Gauss at the equator from just the ratios of the equatorial diameters. The only Galilean moon safe enough to do a landing and EVA on would be Callisto. All other missions would have to be robotic, and even then radiation would mess with the computers.]					[Technical note: NASA has speculated on the feasibility of mining the atmospheres of the outer planets, particularly for helium-3, an isotope of helium that is rare on Earth and could have a very high value per unit mass as thermonuclear fuel.[77] Factories stationed in orbit could mine the gas and deliver it to visiting craft.[79] However, the Jovian system in general poses particular disadvantages for colonization because of the severe radiation conditions prevailing in Jupiter's magnetosphere and the planet's particularly deep gravitational well. 			[Technical note: Other biological dangers of magnetic fields… …cardiac stimulation in the most sensitive population percentile should require 20 times the energy needed for the peripheral nerve stimulation mean. When a static magnetic field is applied to a biological tissue, and ionic currents are present, a net force; applied to moving ions… The effects of EMF on the stimulation of nerve or muscle cells have recently been studied in humans at field strengths as high as 8 T… At the highest field strengths currently available, the flow-induced current densities are below the threshold levels needed to cause nerve or muscle stimulation effects, and no significant vital sign changes, e.g., ECG recordings, have been reported at these high field strengths. ...if the products of a chemical reaction are more paramagnetical than the reactants, the presence of a magnetic field could shift the reaction equilibrium to increase the concentration of the products. A very common and important chemical reaction in humans is the dissociation of oxyhemoglobin (diamagnetic) into separate molecules of oxygen and hemoglobin (both paramagnetic). In this case, an externally applied magnetic field could lower the energy barrier for the dissociation. Calculations indicate that, even in an applied field of 1 T, the free energy barrier to dissociation is changed by only 1 J/mol [36]. Such a small energy shift has less effect on the reaction equilibrium than does a temperature change of 0.01°C. Another chemical effect of the static magnetic field consists of the modification of the kinetics and recombination of radical pairs reactions. Free radicals are supposed to be involved in harmful reactions in biological systems, thus any effect that might increase their reactivity or concentration could produce or enhance a harmful effect [37]. From this observation, the radical pair mechanism has been proposed as a working hypothesis for possible adverse effects of magnetic fields on biological systems. In fact, according to the most accepted theory [38–40], the magnetic field splits the radical pairs into two energy levels, this increases the amount of radicals pairs that escape the recombination reaction [41], i.e., the concentration of free radicals. Experimental research has shown that weak magnetic fields may reduce the second-order decay rate constant of the reaction [42]. Several studies analyzed the effects of magnetic fields on the recombination reaction of radical pairs in micelles and confirmed that an externally applied magnetic field increases the number of radicals escaping the recombination reaction [37, 39, 43]. However, few studies have been performed on biological tissues or on animals and humans. Claims that low magnetic fields damage health have led to extensive medical, chemical and physical research: though no firm evidence of hazards has emerged [44]. …it was reported that the auditory evoked potentials of a subject exposed to a static 0.35 T magnetic field was phase-shifted [24]; the phase shift slowly (15 minutes) returned to normal after termination of the magnetic exposure. However, further studies did not confirm these findings [25, 26]. Pacini, et al. in 1999 [27] described the effects of the static magnetic field generated by a 0.2 T magnetic resonance tomograph on a normal human neuronal cell culture. They observed that after 15 minutes exposure, cells showed dramatic changes of morphology, developing branched dendrites featuring synaptic buttons. …a motion-induced electric field, and it can produce biological effects by disrupting physiological electrical signals of the human body, such as neuronal conduction and biopotentials. ECGs of monkeys exposed to a strong static magnetic field showed field-induced morphological changes in T-wave shape. (In electrocardiography, the T wave represents the repolarization (or recovery) of the ventricles. The interval from the beginning of the QRS complex to the apex of the T wave is referred to as the absolute refractory period.) …these changes were explained by the presence of the electromotive force (EMF) induced by blood flow in a static magnetic field, which is proportional to the quantity we can run into situations where the energy is concentrated in an unexpected and undesirable way, usually by certain types of metal. Under certain conditions this could result in heating of the metal and a burn in the surrounding tissue. MRI uses a combination of magnetic fields and radio waves. MRI generates a net magnetization vector in the human body…the gradient magnetic field, which produces different resonant frequencies for aligned protons, depending on their spatial positions on the gradient axes; these gradient fields allow for the spatial localization of bi-dimensional MRI slices and hence the reconstruction of three dimensional MRI images…the radio-frequency electromagnetic wave, centered at the proton resonant frequency, which rotates the vector…dielectric permittivity of the material…the conductivity…the current…For biological tissues, both the dielectric permittivity and the conductivity are strongly non-linear functions of frequency…at low frequencies, electromagnetic fields interact at the cellular or multicellular level; as frequency progressively increases, bio-electromagnetic interactions occur with the cellular membrane and intracellular organelle, followed by molecular interaction and, finally, at microwave frequencies the field interacts only with water molecules…Materials that cannot be permanently magnetized are characterized by a physical parameter, the magnetic susceptibility (χ), which describes their behavior when placed in a magnetic field…measured by the magnetic dipole moment per unit volume…Materials may be classified into three large groups according to the values of their susceptibility: diamagnetic materials (-1 [ χ [ 0), paramagnetic materials (0 [ χ [ 0.01) and ferromagnetic materials (χ ] 0.01). The safety issues associated with exposure to static magnetic fields have been discussed for more than a century: in 1892 Peterson and Kennelly [18] studied the effects of the exposure to the largest magnet then available (approximately 0.15 T). They exposed a dog and a young boy to the whole-body magnetic field, finding no positive results. About 30 years later, in 1921, Drinker and Thompson [19] investigated possible health consequences of exposure to magnetic fields in industrial workers. They performed numerous experiments in vitro, on nerve-muscle cells, and in vivo, on living animals, and they concluded that the static magnetic field had no significance as a health hazard. Since then, several studies have been performed, and a review [20], published in 1962, collected about 400 reports dealing with biological effects of magnetic fields. According to Schenck [17], the portion of this literature dealing with supposed pathological or therapeutic effects of magnetic fields is contradictory and confusing. Moreover, basic information, such as the field strength and its variation over the body, is not provided. Interest in the biological effects of static magnetic fields has increased with the invention of MRI at the beginning of the 80s. In the last twenty years, several studies were carried out in order to understand the potential hazards associated with exposure to a strong static magnetic field. The majority of these studies did not report positive results, thus postulating no adverse effects for human health. In 1981, Budinger [21] summarized the work done previous to that date, concluding that from an analysis of the vast literature on cell cultures, animals, and men, no experimental protocol was found that, when repeated by other investigators, gave reproducible positive results. Twenty years later, Schenck [17] confirmed this and concluded his review stating that, because of the difficulty in establishing a negative conclusion, it should not be concluded that it has been proven that there are no significant biological effects of static magnetic fields. However, the steadily increasing capability to realize ever stronger magnets gives reason to believe that such effects could eventually be established, but probably at field strengths well above those currently utilized in MRI. In a relatively recent report [22], no adverse biological effects were found after sub-chronic (10 weeks) exposure to a very high magnetic field (9.4 T) in adult male and female rats and in their progeny. There was a statistically significant (p [ 0.05) finding for sensations of nausea, vertigo, and metallic taste in subjects exposed to 1.5 and 4 T static magnetic fields, but no statistical significance was found for other effects such as headache, hiccups, tinnitus, vomiting, and numbness. A higher incidence of positive reports originated from those subjects exposed to the 4 T field. However there was no evidence that these effects were at all harmful.]					[Technical note: Other biological dangers of magnetic fields… …cardiac stimulation in the most sensitive population percentile should require 20 times the energy needed for the peripheral nerve stimulation mean. The interval from the beginning of the QRS complex to the apex of the T wave is referred to as the absolute refractory period.) …these changes were explained by the presence of the electromotive force (EMF) induced by blood flow in a static magnetic field, which is proportional to the quantity we can run into situations where the energy is concentrated in an unexpected and undesirable way, usually by certain types of metal. Under certain conditions this could result in heating of the metal and a burn in the surrounding tissue. MRI uses a combination of magnetic fields and radio waves. MRI generates a net magnetization vector in the human body…the gradient magnetic field, which produces different resonant frequencies for aligned protons, depending on their spatial positions on the gradient axes; these gradient fields allow for the spatial localization of bi-dimensional MRI slices and hence the reconstruction of three dimensional MRI images…the radio-frequency electromagnetic wave, centered at the proton resonant frequency, which rotates the vector…dielectric permittivity of the material…the conductivity…the current…For biological tissues, both the dielectric permittivity and the conductivity are strongly non-linear functions of frequency…at low frequencies, electromagnetic fields interact at the cellular or multicellular level; as frequency progressively increases, bio-electromagnetic interactions occur with the cellular membrane and intracellular organelle, followed by molecular interaction and, finally, at microwave frequencies the field interacts only with water molecules…Materials that cannot be permanently magnetized are characterized by a physical parameter, the magnetic susceptibility (χ), which describes their behavior when placed in a magnetic field…measured by the magnetic dipole moment per unit volume…Materials may be classified into three large groups according to the values of their susceptibility: diamagnetic materials (-1 [ χ [ 0), paramagnetic materials (0 [ χ [ 0.01) and ferromagnetic materials (χ ] 0.01). The safety issues associated with exposure to static magnetic fields have been discussed for more than a century: in 1892 Peterson and Kennelly [18] studied the effects of the exposure to the largest magnet then available (approximately 0.15 T). They exposed a dog and a young boy to the whole-body magnetic field, finding no positive results. About 30 years later, in 1921, Drinker and Thompson [19] investigated possible health consequences of exposure to magnetic fields in industrial workers. They performed numerous experiments in vitro, on nerve-muscle cells, and in vivo, on living animals, and they concluded that the static magnetic field had no significance as a health hazard. Since then, several studies have been performed, and a review [20], published in 1962, collected about 400 reports dealing with biological effects of magnetic fields. According to Schenck [17], the portion of this literature dealing with supposed pathological or therapeutic effects of magnetic fields is contradictory and confusing. Moreover, basic information, such as the field strength and its variation over the body, is not provided. Interest in the biological effects of static magnetic fields has increased with the invention of MRI at the beginning of the 80s. In the last twenty years, several studies were carried out in order to understand the potential hazards associated with exposure to a strong static magnetic field. The majority of these studies did not report positive results, thus postulating no adverse effects for human health. In 1981, Budinger [21] summarized the work done previous to that date, concluding that from an analysis of the vast literature on cell cultures, animals, and men, no experimental protocol was found that, when repeated by other investigators, gave reproducible positive results. Twenty years later, Schenck [17] confirmed this and concluded his review stating that, because of the difficulty in establishing a negative conclusion, it should not be concluded that it has been proven that there are no significant biological effects of static magnetic fields. However, the steadily increasing capability to realize ever stronger magnets gives reason to believe that such effects could eventually be established, but probably at field strengths well above those currently utilized in MRI. In a relatively recent report [22], no adverse biological effects were found after sub-chronic (10 weeks) exposure to a very high magnetic field (9.4 T) in adult male and female rats and in their progeny. There was a statistically significant (p [ 0.05) finding for sensations of nausea, vertigo, and metallic taste in subjects exposed to 1.5 and 4 T static magnetic fields, but no statistical significance was found for other effects such as headache, hiccups, tinnitus, vomiting, and numbness. A higher incidence of positive reports originated from those subjects exposed to the 4 T field. However there was no evidence that these effects were at all harmful.]											
			[Technical note: Rogue planets have been ejected from their planetary system. We investigate the possibility that a rogue planet could maintain a liquid ocean under layers of thermally-insulating water ice and frozen atmosphere as a result of geothermal heat flux. We find that a rogue planet of Earth-like composition and age could maintain a subglacial liquid ocean if it were ~3.5 times more massive than Earth. If a rogue planet had about ten times higher water mass fraction or a thick cryo-atmospheric layer, it would need to be only ~0.3 times the mass of Earth to maintain a liquid ocean. Such a planet could be detected from reflected solar radiation and its thermal emission could be characterized in the far-IR if it passed within O(1000) AU of Earth.]					[Technical note: Rogue planets have been ejected from their planetary system. 			```The greater part of its plumage was of an intense cinnabar red, with a gloss as of spun glass, while springing from each side of the breast were little tufts of greyish feathers terminated by a broad band of intense emerald green. Adorning this little bird were two middle tail feathers modified into very slender wirelike shafts, each bearing at the extremity a web coiled into a perfect spiral disc of emerald green. The beauty and brilliancy of this insect are indescribable, and on taking it out of my net and opening the glorious wings, my heart began to beat violently, the blood rushed to my head, and I felt much more like fainting than I have done when in apprehension of immediate death. I gazed upwards and saw a large mass of something overhead which resolved itself into a large snake, compactly coiled up in a kind of knot; I had slept soundly all night directly under him. His face and a terrible wound in his head were a solid mass of flies, and thousands of insects were crawling over the blood clots on the stones beside him; it did not seem possible that a human being could live under such conditions, and yet the bystanders told us that he had been lying there for thirty hours. In the hospital compound we met a chair in which was lying an old man groaning loudly and dripping with blood; his poor wife was crying quietly and, between her sobs, was offering the wounded man mustard pickles from a small dish in her hand, believing food would cure all ills. One dog was ripped wide open, another received a horn-thrust in the side, and the big red leader was thrown over a cliff to the rocks below. Hotenfa carried him in his arms and laid him gently on a blanket in the temple, but the splendid animal died during the night. The bee-hunter rapidly got up—thirty, forty, fifty feet above the ground—climbing with as much coolness and apparent certainty as if he were going up a ladder, until he drew his knife and cut off the comb at one slice close to the tree. Caldwell and I were on our knees over the trap when suddenly a low rumbling growl came from the grass not twenty feet away. Suddenly at the left and just below us there came the faintest crunching sound as a loose stone shifted under a heavy weight, but the blue tiger had slipped back into the heart of the lair. He seemed the very spirit of the mountains, a thing born of peaks and crags, vibrant with the breath of the clouds. Should civilized man ever reach these distant lands, we may be sure that he will so disturb the nicely-balanced relations of organic and inorganic nature as to cause the disappearance, and finally the extinction, of these very beings. Our vast manufacturing system, our gigantic commerce, our crowded towns and cities, support and continually renew a mass of human misery and crime absolutely greater than has ever existed before. We allow over a hundred thousand persons known to have no means of subsistence but by crime to remain at large and prey upon the community; this, in a country which boasts of its mechanical skill and scientific knowledge, I can but term a state of social barbarism. As Yvette turned from the window her eyes were wet with unshed tears, and a lump had risen in my throat; not all the pleasures of the city could make us wish to end the wild, free life of the year gone by. The spot was redolent with the atmosphere of the lazy East; the East which, like the fabled "Lorelei," weaves a mystic spell about the wanderer whom she has loved and taken to her heart.					```The greater part of its plumage was of an intense cinnabar red, with a gloss as of spun glass, while springing from each side of the breast were little tufts of greyish feathers terminated by a broad band of intense emerald green. Adorning this little bird were two middle tail feathers modified into very slender wirelike shafts, each bearing at the extremity a web coiled into a perfect spiral disc of emerald green. The beauty and brilliancy of this insect are indescribable, and on taking it out of my net and opening the glorious wings, my heart began to beat violently, the blood rushed to my head, and I felt much more like fainting than I have done when in apprehension of immediate death. I gazed upwards and saw a large mass of something overhead which resolved itself into a large snake, compactly coiled up in a kind of knot; I had slept soundly all night directly under him. His face and a terrible wound in his head were a solid mass of flies, and thousands of insects were crawling over the blood clots on the stones beside him; it did not seem possible that a human being could live under such conditions, and yet the bystanders told us that he had been lying there for thirty hours. In the hospital compound we met a chair in which was lying an old man groaning loudly and dripping with blood; his poor wife was crying quietly and, between her sobs, was offering the wounded man mustard pickles from a small dish in her hand, believing food would cure all ills. One dog was ripped wide open, another received a horn-thrust in the side, and the big red leader was thrown over a cliff to the rocks below. Hotenfa carried him in his arms and laid him gently on a blanket in the temple, but the splendid animal died during the night. The bee-hunter rapidly got up—thirty, forty, fifty feet above the ground—climbing with as much coolness and apparent certainty as if he were going up a ladder, until he drew his knife and cut off the comb at one slice close to the tree. Caldwell and I were on our knees over the trap when suddenly a low rumbling growl came from the grass not twenty feet away. Suddenly at the left and just below us there came the faintest crunching sound as a loose stone shifted under a heavy weight, but the blue tiger had slipped back into the heart of the lair. He seemed the very spirit of the mountains, a thing born of peaks and crags, vibrant with the breath of the clouds. Should civilized man ever reach these distant lands, we may be sure that he will so disturb the nicely-balanced relations of organic and inorganic nature as to cause the disappearance, and finally the extinction, of these very beings. Our vast manufacturing system, our gigantic commerce, our crowded towns and cities, support and continually renew a mass of human misery and crime absolutely greater than has ever existed before. We allow over a hundred thousand persons known to have no means of subsistence but by crime to remain at large and prey upon the community; this, in a country which boasts of its mechanical skill and scientific knowledge, I can but term a state of social barbarism. As Yvette turned from the window her eyes were wet with unshed tears, and a lump had risen in my throat; not all the pleasures of the city could make us wish to end the wild, free life of the year gone by. The spot was redolent with the atmosphere of the lazy East; the East which, like the fabled "Lorelei," weaves a mystic spell about the wanderer whom she has loved and taken to her heart.

			Across various Asian countries, the New Wave movements emerged at different times, each influenced by technological advancements and local contexts. In Japan, the Japanese New Wave of the 1960s saw filmmakers like Nagisa Oshima and Yasujirō Ozu challenging traditional storytelling techniques. Oshima's "In the Realm of the Senses" (1976) pushed the boundaries of eroticism and censorship. In Hong Kong, the Hong Kong New Wave of the 1980s saw the rise of directors like Wong Kar-wai and John Woo, who introduced stylized visuals and kinetic action in films like "Chungking Express" (1994) and "The Killer" (1989). In Taiwan, the Taiwanese New Wave of the 1980s brought forth filmmakers like Hou Hsiao-Hsien and Edward Yang, who delved into intimate and reflective storytelling in films like "A City of Sadness" (1989) and "Yi Yi" (2000). 			CONTRAST is EVERYTHING. The key to keeping the ear pleased is to constantly be introducing new elements and directly contrasting what has come before. Therefore, just like how I outlined the importance of repetition in my last point, the next most important thing to do is IMMEDIATELY contrast your repetition with something dramatically different, both rhythmically and melodically. Example: if you start with longer, legato notes, go to shorter, staccato notes in a completely different register. This principle is applied within the melodic phrases themselves, as well as in a more macro way with the different sections of a song. ==========================================================================================
 MACHINE - DO NOT EDIT
==========================================================================================
 convert an array of tab lines to an object the machine can work with
def to_bar_hash(ar)
 ar.inject (Hash.new('')) do | all, current |
 char, rest = current.tr(' |', '').split(':')
 all[char] += rest
 all
 end
end

 split tabs into separate bars
def parse(tabs)
 return tabs.split( \n )
 .chunk { | line | line.include? '|' }
 .select { | k, v | v[0].include? '|' }
 .map { | k, v | to_bar_hash(v) }
end

bars = parse(tabs)

bars.each do | bar |
 Assume all lines in a bar is as long as the first one
 length = bar.first[1].length
 length.times do | n |
 instruments.each do | key, sounds |
 note = bar[key][n]
 sample sounds[note] if sounds[note]
 end
 sleep time
 end
end

 END DRUM TAB CONVERTER

 HELPER: Convert named chord symbols to MIDI note arrays

define :named_chord_to_notes do |name|
 chord_map = {
 :C => chord(:C4, :major).to_a,
 :Cm => chord(:C4, :minor).to_a,
 :C7 => chord(:C4, :dom7).to_a,
 :Cm7 => chord(:C4, :m7).to_a,
 :D => chord(:D4, :major).to_a,
 :Dm => chord(:D4, :minor).to_a,
 :D7 => chord(:D4, :dom7).to_a,
 :Dm7 => chord(:D4, :m7).to_a,
 :E => chord(:E4, :major).to_a,
 :Em => chord(:E4, :minor).to_a,
 :E7 => chord(:E4, :dom7).to_a,
 :Em7 => chord(:E4, :m7).to_a,
 :F => chord(:F4, :major).to_a,
 :Fm => chord(:F4, :minor).to_a,
 :F7 => chord(:F4, :dom7).to_a,
 :G => chord(:G4, :major).to_a,
 :Gm => chord(:G4, :minor).to_a,
 :G7 => chord(:G4, :dom7).to_a,
 :A => chord(:A4, :major).to_a,
 :Am => chord(:A4, :minor).to_a,
 :A7 => chord(:A4, :dom7).to_a,
 :B => chord(:B4, :major).to_a,
 :Bm => chord(:B4, :minor).to_a,
 :B7 => chord(:B4, :dom7).to_a
 }
 chord_map[name]
end

			Early European art music developed through embellishment of a single line of melody and classical theory still emphasises the correct "horizontal" progress of single-note parts, sometimes known as "voice-leading". Generally, to the melody in the upper part is added first a bass line and then two inner lines to complete the chords in four part harmony suitable for a choir or string section, terminating with cadences, avoiding some chord inversions and favouring others, maintaining an orderly and melodic conjunct, contrary and oblique motion of each part relative to the others in order to achieve unity of texture by avoidance of inappropriate intervals, parallel fifths and octaves etc. Much practice is given to the art of harmonic transition and development that is essential to classical music's use of harmony as a means of achieving unity in a large-scale form. Although, as noted above, classical music has its cliche progressions these are seldom named and discussed: perhaps only Schoenberg among the authors of popular text-books of harmony has made some attempt to do so. 			Folk and blues tunes frequently use the Mixolydian scale, which has a flat seventh degree, altering the position of the three major chords to I - Flat VII-IV. ==========================================================================================
 MACHINE - DO NOT EDIT
==========================================================================================
 convert an array of tab lines to an object the machine can work with
def to_bar_hash(ar)
 ar.inject (Hash.new('')) do | all, current |
 char, rest = current.tr(' |', '').split(':')
 all[char] += rest
 all
 end
end

 split tabs into separate bars
def parse(tabs)
 return tabs.split( \n )
 .chunk { | line | line.include? '|' }
 .select { | k, v | v[0].include? '|' }
 .map { | k, v | to_bar_hash(v) }
end

bars = parse(tabs)

bars.each do | bar |
 Assume all lines in a bar is as long as the first one
 length = bar.first[1].length
 length.times do | n |
 instruments.each do | key, sounds |
 note = bar[key][n]
 sample sounds[note] if sounds[note]
 end
 sleep time
 end
end

 You can also mix named chord and note arrays

start_chord_input = :F7
target_chord_input = [:G4, :B4, :D5]

========================================================
 INSTRUCTIONS
 Enter your start and target chords here.
 You can use:
 1) Named chord symbols (:C, :Dm7, :Fs7, :Cm11, etc.)
 2) Arrays of MIDI notes ([60, 64, 67], [:C4, :E4, :G4])
 3) A mix of the two

 EXAMPLE INPUT
 start_chord_input = :F7
 target_chord_input = [:G4, :B4, :D5]

========================================================
 HELPER: Convert named chord symbols to MIDI note arrays
========================================================

define :named_chord_to_notes do |name|
 chord_map = {
 :C => chord(:C4, :major).to_a,
 :Cm => chord(:C4, :minor).to_a,
 :C7 => chord(:C4, :dom7).to_a,
 :Cm7 => chord(:C4, :m7).to_a,
 :D => chord(:D4, :major).to_a,
 :Dm => chord(:D4, :minor).to_a,
 :D7 => chord(:D4, :dom7).to_a,
 :Dm7 => chord(:D4, :m7).to_a,
 :E => chord(:E4, :major).to_a,
 :Em => chord(:E4, :minor).to_a,
 :E7 => chord(:E4, :dom7).to_a,
 :Em7 => chord(:E4, :m7).to_a,
 :F => chord(:F4, :major).to_a,
 :Fm => chord(:F4, :minor).to_a,
 :F7 => chord(:F4, :dom7).to_a,
 :G => chord(:G4, :major).to_a,
 :Gm => chord(:G4, :minor).to_a,
 :G7 => chord(:G4, :dom7).to_a,
 :A => chord(:A4, :major).to_a,
 :Am => chord(:A4, :minor).to_a,
 :A7 => chord(:A4, :dom7).to_a,
 :B => chord(:B4, :major).to_a,
 :Bm => chord(:B4, :minor).to_a,
 :B7 => chord(:B4, :dom7).to_a
 }
 chord_map[name]
end

			Max believes that a great chorus feels like you've "already heard it" once you arrive at it. This is accomplished a few different ways. The main one is by using the verse to setup the chorus, by foreshadowing it with some of the same elements or phrases. The most extreme version of this is actually using the EXACT same melody in the verse and the chorus. Max likes to use the example "Let's Go Crazy" by Prince to demonstrate this, where Prince's chorus is the exact same melody as the verse. Max often does this much more subtly, however, by merely hinting at or referencing the chorus melody in the verse. He also applies this to verse chorus lyrics. You'll notice in many of his songs that the song title appears in the verse somewhere, as well as in the chorus. This is intentional.					Hell, and you

			My last point is about range, and having a good understanding of scales and the notes available to you in a given key. Max and his team often write very simple melodies that use maybe 3 or 4 notes at a time. But throughout the course of an entire song, they utilize the full range of the given key as much as possible. If one section is in a certain register, another section will be in a very different register, and then another section will be in a very different register altogether. Many writers tend to run over the same notes within the same range in a key over and over throughout a song, wearing them out essentially, and causing our ears to get bored. Experiment with going up high, then low. Use the full range of whatever key you're in and explore it. And also be very aware of how to properly resolve melodies when the chords call for it. 			Repetition Penalty					into a grammar											
			Repetition, especially while the chords are changing underneath, is key to making a melodic idea "hooky." You will notice this technique over and over in Max Martin songs. They find that magical melodic phrase that grabs you, and repeat the same phrase over and over, while the chords are changing underneath it. This has the effect of changing the quality of the notes in your melody with each new chord, which is very pleasing to the ears brain. You're hearing the same melody repeated multiple times, but the chords are changing how it's resonating. Many people write long, meandering melodies that are not memorable because there isn't enough repetition of key moments. Try singing even just one note sustained, and play different chords under it (in the correct key, obviously). Notice how the quality or "feeling" of that single note changes as you do that. Learn to implement that same effect with more complex melodic ideas.					into a loop that wouldn't quit.

Introducing the ii chord into these progressions emphasises their appeal as constituting elementary forms of circle progression. These, named for the circle of fifths, consist of "adjacent roots in ascending fourth or descending fifth relationship"—for instance, the sequence vi - ii - V - I ascends with each successive chord to one a fourth above the previous. Such a motion, based upon close harmonic relations, offers "undoubtedly the most common and the strongest of all harmonic progressions".[8] The succession of cadences gives an impression of inevitable return to the key-note of the piece.

			The Andalusian cadence comes from the Southern region of Spain and is most traditionally tied to Flamenco music. It’s one of the most dramatic chord progressions due to its clear descending motion and use of the major V chord.					Meaning, it creates a sense of unresolved tension and gloom that people really cling to and respond to.											
			The Andalusian Cadence is named after the Andalusia region in Spain, where it was used in flamenco music. In A minor, this dramatic minor progression contains the following chords: Am-G-F-E. Notice that we raise the seventh note (G to G) on the E chord. This raised seventh adds that distinct Spanish flavor.					Meaning:

Max and his team often write very simple melodies that use maybe 3 or 4 notes at a time. But throughout the course of an entire song, they utilize the full range of the given key as much as possible. If one section is in a certain register, another section will be in a very different register, and then another section will be in a very different register altogether. Many writers tend to run over the same notes within the same range in a key over and over throughout a song, wearing them out essentially, and causing our ears to get bored. Experiment with going up high, then low. Use the full range of whatever key you're in and explore it. And also be very aware of how to properly resolve melodies when the chords call for it.

			What does that mean? Well, when you think gothic novel, think Scooby-Doo. This cartoon is one of the only surviving storylines that still follows that outmoded style. See, the gothic novel arose in the hyper-rationalist era of the mid 1700s, when educated society (read: the people who bought books) considered any lip service to the old superstitious ghosts-and-goblin days to be a sort of a blasphemy against the newly-forming scientism. A writer who wanted to write ghost stories could kiss his patron goodbye. But, of course there will always be people who are interested in the mystical side of the human experience. So, the gothic form originated a way of sneaking fantasy elements in your stories without making yourself look like an unenlightened rube. It works like this: You write your ghosts-and-goblins story and fill it with as much mysticism and mumbo-jumbo as you please. Then, at the end, you catch the bad guy, the mask is removed, and it's "Zoinks, Scooby I guess it wasn't ghosts and goblins after all, it was just Monsignor Otranto behind the special mirror the whole time." All is explained…you got your spooky fantasy story with your happy rationalist ending. But this was a short-lived thing. Pretty soon, the Romance movement got into full swing, the gothic genre split. Some writers, free from the bonds of rationalist explanations produced works, like the old vampire tales and ghost stories, that were truly fantasy. Other writers pursued the rationalist side full swing and wrote the amazing early works of science fiction, in which we are expected to interpret the fantastic plot devices as fully-explainable scientific phenomena. The writers of Scooby-Doo are the only ones who still walk the line between fantasy and reality for the whole story, then explain it all away at the end.					play choose([:e1, :g1]), release: 1, amp: amp_val if one_in(3)

			Your physics optics + creative storytelling + pedagogy combo allows you to prototype and implement interactive experiences independently					Repetition, especially while the chords are changing underneath, is key to making a melodic idea "hooky." You will notice this technique over and over in Max Martin songs. They find that magical melodic phrase that grabs you, and repeat the same phrase over and over, while the chords are changing underneath it. This has the effect of changing the quality of the notes in your melody with each new chord, which is very pleasing to the ears brain. You're hearing the same melody repeated multiple times, but the chords are changing how it's resonating. Many people write long, meandering melodies that are not memorable because there isn't enough repetition of key moments. Try singing even just one note sustained, and play different chords under it (in the correct key, obviously). Notice how the quality or "feeling" of that single note changes as you do that. Learn to implement that same effect with more complex melodic ideas.

			ပြီးတော့ ဒေါသတကြီး။					RMS (Radical Minimal Skepticism) is a framework that confines knowledge strictly to direct perception, rejecting any claim that extends beyond what can be immediately experienced.											
			ပြီးတော့ ပြန်လည်တွေ့ရှိခံရ။					RMS (Radical Minimal Skepticism) is a framework that strictly confines knowledge to direct perception, rejecting any claim that extends beyond what can be immediately experienced.											
			ပြီးတော့ ပြောပြဖို့ ဘယ်သူမှလည်း မကျန်တော့ဘူး။					RMS also establishes a taxonomy of perception, categorizing experiences based on their Clarity, Granularity, Coherence, and Control rather than external assumptions about their causes. Instead of sorting perceptions into traditional philosophical categories (such as “real” vs. “illusory”), RMS classifies them solely by how they present themselves in experience.											
			ပြီးတော့ ရိုးရှင်းစွာပဲ။ မြေအောက်ခန်းကြမ်းပြင်က					RMS doesn’t try to guess what’s “real” or “illusory.” It just sorts perceptions by Clarity, Granularity, Coherence, and Control—qualities of experience itself, without making assumptions about what’s behind it.											
			ပလာစမာ-ပေကျင်း၊ ကျွန်ုပ်ရဲ့ ပန်းနာရင်ကျပ်ရောဂါ။					RMS is a framework that strictly confines knowledge to direct perception, rejecting any claim that extends beyond what can be immediately experienced. It operates on the principle of equivalence: if two ideas cannot be distinguished by any conceivable test, they are functionally identical.											
			ပိန်လှီ၊ ဖျားနာ၊ အဝတ်ဗလာ၊					RMS positions itself between realism and solipsism, asserting that indistinguishable propositions are equivalent. It emphasizes being cautious about claims that go beyond direct perception or evidence. This makes the worldview more extreme, highlighting the limits of knowledge based on what we can perceive directly.											
			ပိုကောင်း-အတူတူ၊					RMS starts with the equivalence principle: if two propositions are indistinguishable by any conceivable test, they’re the same. From that, the supposed distinctions between direct and indirect experience (DIU), interior and exterior (IEI), and so on, start to break down. What we’re left with is a reality shaped entirely by perception—each person constructing their own taxonomy of what counts as real.											
			ပိုပြီး လွတ်လပ်ကြ၊ ပိုပြီး ကြီးမားကြတယ်။					RMS starts with the equivalence principle: if two propositions are indistinguishable by any conceivable test, they’re the same. From there, the supposed distinctions we take for granted start to unravel. The ADU (Actual Distilled Unity) forces us to question whether abstraction dilutes reality or just reframes it. The QPU (Qualitative Positional Unity) reminds us that what something is can’t be separated from where and when it is. Strip away the illusions, and all that’s left is perception—each person assembling their own taxonomy of what counts as real.											
			ပုံသွင်းထားတဲ့ ခက်ရင်း၊ ဝက်သားအရေပြားကြော် (pork-crackling)၊					RMS starts with the equivalence principle: if two propositions are indistinguishable by any conceivable test, they’re the same. From there, things start to get weird. The IEU (Interior Exterior Unity) challenges whether anything truly exists “out there” beyond perception, or if all experience is just an internal construct. The ADU (Agent Determinism Unity) dissolves the line between free will and inevitability—after all, if every choice is indistinguishable from the circumstances that led to it, are we really choosing? The QPU (Qualia Phenomenology Unity) breaks down the idea that subjective experience and objective reality are separate things—what you see is what’s real, at least as far as you can tell.

The name of the territory is in dispute. Under Russian authority, it’s been referred to variously as the Republic of Sakha, or the Autonomous Republic of Sakha. However, the independence fighters refer to the area as Yakutia. There have long been rumblings for independence from the indigenous Sakha/Yakut people, but it wasn’t until the ethnic Russians, who dominate the area, decided they want independence from Moscow that the conflict really boiled over. These Sakha Russians take on the mantle of Yakut independence in their propaganda and  but generally treat the yakut people as a political soccer ball. Thus the sides, broadly speaking, are: Moscow-loyalist Russians vs Pro-independence Sakha Russians. Ironically, most Yakuts are now against independence. Yakut ethnic extremism was once a rare, very fringe phenomenon, but it was very violent when it did happen. However, in the decade before the Sakha rebellion, the Yakuts were radicalized by neighboring Buryats whose own independence movement flared on and off for years before burning out with no resolution due to sheer exhaustion of forces. Despite promises to the contrary, Yakuts generally fear the Sakha Russians will gain even more power in an independent state. However, some Yakuts, especially young men, do side with the independence movement and form a large chunk of the fighters. Many of them realize they’ve gotten in over their heads. Various other Siberian ethnic minorities have mostly tried to stay neutral, although many individuals may side with one group or another. These include the (thoroughly russified) Itelmen, who tend to side with Moscow, the Evens who mostly side with the Yakuts, and the Koryaks/Chukchis who have largely tried to keep out of the fray.

			worcester ma indie					What does that mean? Well, when you think gothic novel, think Scooby-Doo. This cartoon is one of the only surviving storylines that still follows that outmoded style. See, the gothic novel arose in the hyper-rationalist era of the mid 1700s, when educated society (read: the people who bought books) considered any lip service to the old superstitious ghosts-and-goblin days to be a sort of a blasphemy against the newly-forming scientism. A writer who wanted to write ghost stories could kiss his patron goodbye. But, of course there will always be people who are interested in the mystical side of the human experience. So, the gothic form originated a way of sneaking fantasy elements in your stories without making yourself look like an unenlightened rube. It works like this: You write your ghosts-and-goblins story and fill it with as much mysticism and mumbo-jumbo as you please. Then, at the end, you catch the bad guy, the mask is removed, and it's "Zoinks, Scooby I guess it wasn't ghosts and goblins after all, it was just Monsignor Otranto behind the special mirror the whole time." All is explained…you got your spooky fantasy story with your happy rationalist ending. But this was a short-lived thing. Pretty soon, the Romance movement got into full swing, the gothic genre split. Some writers, free from the bonds of rationalist explanations produced works, like the old vampire tales and ghost stories, that were truly fantasy. Other writers pursued the rationalist side full swing and wrote the amazing early works of science fiction, in which we are expected to interpret the fantastic plot devices as fully-explainable scientific phenomena. The writers of Scooby-Doo are the only ones who still walk the line between fantasy and reality for the whole story, then explain it all away at the end.
